title: The Reef That Loses Its Colour
paragraphs: A coral reef looks like a garden of stone, but it is built by animals. Each coral polyp grows a hard skeleton, and millions of skeletons together form the reef. Inside the tissues of most reef corals live tiny algae. The algae use sunlight to make sugars, and they pass much of this food to their host. They also give the coral most of its colour. This partnership is so productive that reefs can flourish in clear tropical water where food is scarce.

When the sea stays warmer than usual, the partnership breaks down. The stressed coral expels the algae, and the white skeleton shows through its clear tissue. Scientists call this bleaching. A bleached coral is not dead, but it has lost its main source of food. If the water cools soon enough, the algae can return and the colour comes back. If the heat lasts, the weakened animal may die.

Reefs matter far beyond their beauty. They shelter a remarkable share of ocean species, and they absorb the force of waves before it reaches the shore. The Great Barrier Reef has suffered several mass bleaching events since the late nineteen nineties. Reefs can regrow, yet recovery needs time without new heat stress, and repeated heat leaves less time between shocks.
